verses.text: After saying goodbye, we sailed straight to Cos. The next day we reached Rhodes, and from there Patara.
We found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, boarded it, and sailed away.
We came into view of Cyprus, passed it to our left, and sailed on to Syria. We landed at Tyre, where the ship was unloading its cargo.
We found the disciples there and stayed seven days. Through the Spirit they kept telling Paul not to go to Jerusalem.
When our time there was up, we continued the journey. All the disciples, with their wives and children, came with us outside the city. We knelt on the beach and prayed together.
After saying goodbye, we boarded the ship, and they went back home.
We completed the voyage from Tyre and arrived at Ptolemais. We greeted the believers there and stayed with them for one day.
The next day we left and came to Caesarea. We stayed at the home of Philip the evangelist, one of the Seven.
He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
We had been there for several days when a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came over, took Paul’s belt, tied his own feet and hands with it, and said, “The Holy Spirit says: ‘This is how the Jews in Jerusalem will tie up the man who owns this belt and hand him over to the Gentiles.’”
When we heard this, we and the local believers begged Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
But Paul answered, “Why are you crying and breaking my heart? I’m ready not only to be tied up in Jerusalem but also to die there for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
When he wouldn’t be persuaded, we stopped arguing and said, “May the Lord’s will be done.”
After those days, we packed up and went to Jerusalem.
Some disciples from Caesarea went with us and brought us to Mnason from Cyprus, an early disciple, whose home would host us.
When we reached Jerusalem, the believers welcomed us warmly.
The next day Paul went with us to see James, and all the elders were there.
After greeting them, Paul gave a detailed report of what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
When they heard it, they praised God. Then they said to Paul, “Brother, you can see that thousands of Jews have believed, and they are all deeply committed to the Law.
“They’ve been told that you teach Jews living among the Gentiles to abandon Moses—that you tell them not to circumcise their children or follow our customs.
“What should we do? They will certainly hear that you’ve arrived, and the whole group will come together.
“So do what we tell you. Four men here have taken a vow.

“Go with them and complete the purification rite. Pay their expenses so they can have their heads shaved. Then everyone will know the reports about you aren’t true and that you also live in obedience to the Law.
“As for Gentile believers, we have sent them our decision: they should avoid food sacrificed to idols, blood, meat from strangled animals, and sexual immorality.”

The next day Paul took the men and joined them in the purification rite. Then he went into the temple to announce when the days of purification would end and the offering would be made for each of them.
When the seven days were almost over, some Jews from Asia saw Paul in the temple. They stirred up the crowd and seized him.

They shouted, “People of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against our people, the Law, and this place. He has even brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place!”
They had seen Trophimus the Ephesian with Paul in the city and assumed Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred up. People rushed together, grabbed Paul, and dragged him out of the temple. The doors were shut at once.
As the crowd was trying to kill Paul, word reached the Roman commander that all Jerusalem was in an uproar.
He immediately took soldiers and centurions and ran down to the crowd. When the people saw the commander and soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
The commander came over, arrested Paul, and ordered him chained with two chains. Then he asked who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd shouted one accusation, others another. Since the noise made it impossible to learn the facts, the commander ordered Paul taken to the barracks.
When Paul reached the steps, the soldiers had to carry him because the crowd was so violent.
The crowd followed, shouting, “Get rid of him!”
As Paul was about to be taken into the barracks, he asked the commander, “May I say something to you?” The commander replied, “You speak Greek?
“Aren’t you the Egyptian who recently started a revolt and led four thousand men of the Assassins into the wilderness?”
Paul answered, “I’m a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of a respected city. Please let me speak to the people.”
When the commander gave him permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned with his hand for the crowd to be quiet. When they fell silent, he spoke to them in Hebrew.
